title: Three Suggestions per Keystroke
statement:
A search box knows a list of distinct products. The user types typed one character at a time. After each character, the box shows up to three products that start with everything typed so far, choosing the alphabetically smallest ones and listing them in alphabetical order.

Return a list with one entry per typed character: the suggestions shown after that character. An entry is empty when no product starts with that prefix.

examples.why: "m" and "mo" match all five; the three smallest are shown. After "mou" only two products are left.
Once "cx" matches nothing, every longer prefix also matches nothing.
A product equal to the prefix itself counts, and "a" sorts before "ab". The input order of products does not matter.

constraints: All strings are lowercase letters; products are distinct
hints: Sorting the products first means "the three smallest that match" are simply the first three matches you meet.
In a sorted list, all products with a given prefix sit next to each other. Binary search can find where that block starts.
Or build a trie from the sorted products and store, at every node, the first three words that pass through it. Then typing is just walking down one node per character.

explain.intuition:
This is the autocomplete dropdown you have built in a frontend app, done properly. The key observation is that once the products are sorted, every prefix's matches form one contiguous block, and the first three items of that block are exactly the answer.

A trie makes it direct. Insert the products in sorted order, and at every node keep a list of at most three words that pass through it. Because insertion is in sorted order, the first three to arrive are the smallest three. Answering a keystroke is then one step down the trie. If a step falls off the trie, every later prefix is empty as well.
steps: Insert each product into a trie. At every node on its path, append the word to that node's top list if the list has fewer than three entries.
Walk the trie along typed. After each character, output the current node's top list.
Once a character has no child, output an empty list for it and for every remaining character.
pitfalls: Taking the first three matches in input order instead of alphabetical order.
Stopping the output early when a prefix stops matching. The result needs one entry for every typed character.
Forgetting that a product equal to the prefix (like "a" for prefix "a") is a match.

complexity.time: O(S log n) to sort plus O(S) to build, where S is total product length; O(L) to answer

solutions.title: Sort, then filter for each prefix
solutions.idea: After sorting, scan the whole list for every prefix and keep the first three matches.

solutions.title: Sort + binary search for the block
solutions.idea: In sorted order the matches for a prefix are contiguous. Binary search for the first string not smaller than the prefix and look at the next three.

solutions.title: Trie with the top three at every node
solutions.idea: Insert sorted products into a trie; each node remembers the first three words that pass through it. Typing walks down one node per character.

followups: Rank suggestions by popularity instead of alphabetically. What would each trie node store?
The product list changes while the user types. Which of the three approaches handles inserts best?
